drhp.business: GTL Infrastructure provides passive telecommunications infrastructure services — telecom tower sites hosted on a shared basis for telecom operators — and does not undertake manufacturing activities. Its customers are a limited number of major Indian telecom operators, with whom it runs a Customer Governance Framework and Key Account Management structure at corporate and operating-circle level covering network uptime, energy management and project execution. It has been transitioning eligible sites to a maintenance takeover (MTO) contract with one customer, under which reimbursement and …
drhp.expansion: No capacity or network-expansion project is disclosed. Activity is energy optimisation at existing tower sites: a phase-wise roll-out of Li-ion (LFP) battery banks to cut diesel-generator run hours, new grid (EB) connections at 28 previously diesel-dependent sites, and proof-of-concept trials of Li-ion batteries to replace lead-acid batteries and diesel generators at high-consumption sites. The Directors' Report states capital investment on energy conservation equipment as 'Not Applicable'. Under the maintenance takeover (MTO) contract, energy-related capex is incurred directly by the …

litigation.note: MD&A Risk Management section: the trustee of the Series A FCCB has filed a commercial suit before the Bombay High Court for recovery; DRT proceedings remain pending with respect to Rupee Term Loan lenders; property-tax demands on towers are disputed and some payments made under protest. A long-running vendor arbitration was amicably settled and withdrawn, and NCLT/DRT proceedings by two settled lenders were withdrawn. The auditors flagged a material uncertainty related to going concern (Directors' Report).

risks.note: Major operators have shrunk from about 18 to about 4; per TRAI data as of June 2026, Reliance Jio, Bharti Airtel and VIL hold about 92.7% of wireless subscribers, and BSNL most of the rest. That ties revenue to the network strategy, finances and commercial decisions of a few customers.
risks.risk: Customer concentration in a consolidated operator market

risks.note: Reliance Jio has interests in Summit Digital Infrastructure and Bharti Airtel has a strategic stake in Indus Towers; both are expected to favour those providers for new tenancies, which may limit new tenancies for the Company.
risks.risk: New tenancies go to operator-aligned tower companies

risks.note: Operator consolidation already caused co-location churn and large tenancy exits, and operators may still exit, relocate or consolidate sites when contractual lock-ins expire.
risks.risk: Tenancy exits when lock-in periods expire

risks.note: As a vendor to a few operators, the Company is exposed to delayed collections and disputed deductions, and operators' finances vary widely. A settlement and the resolved FEM disputes reduced immediate collection risk, but the Company says concentration and recovery remain material risks.

Liquidity depends on tenancy levels, customer payment cycles, energy and rental costs, statutory demands and the timing of lender settlements. DRT proceedings by Rupee Term Loan lenders are pending, and delays in collections, property monetisation or settlements could hurt the Company's ability to meet its obligations.

Operator exits left liabilities on unoccupied sites with no matching revenue. Unauthorised dismantling and theft persist until those liabilities are resolved; 362 unoccupied sites were dismantled during FY 2025-26.
risks.risk: Liabilities on unoccupied sites, and dismantling or theft of towers

risks.note: The auditors raised a material uncertainty related to going concern (explained in Note 57). Management states it has no intention to discontinue operations.

Revenue depends on a capital-intensive sector driven by spectrum costs, regulation, technology cycles and operator finances. VIL's network expansion still depends on continued access to funding despite AGR relief.
risks.risk: Dependence on the Indian telecom sector and weaker operators' funding

themes.title: Telecom & digital-infrastructure capex
themes.need: 5G monetization, FTTH and tower/fibre densification drive the connectivity cycle - and Q1FY27 repriced the optical leg outright. STLTECH booked order intake of INR 13,100cr in ONE quarter, 1.7x its entire FY26 order book, anchored by a multi-year $1.1bn hyperscaler deal running through FY29, taking the open order book to INR 18,618cr (up 2.4x QoQ) on revenue of INR 1,910cr (+87%) and EBITDA INR 397cr (+184%). It then raised guidance twice on the same call - EBITDA margin target from 20%-by-end-FY27 (already hit at 20.8% in Q1) to 23%, and Data-Center + Enterprise mix from 30% to 50% of FY27 revenue, after DC went from 1% of revenue in FY26 to 21%. The catch is supply, not demand: ex the anchor deal quarterly intake fell to ~INR 3,000cr from INR 7,000-8,000cr because 'we have to pick and choose the orders basis the capacity availability', with germanium and helium named as binding raw-material constraints. BHARTIARTL on ARPU + 5G; INDUSTOWER on tower rollout; SUYOG-tier on passive infra; GTPL/HFCL-tier on broadband + fibre; tariff hikes and rural FTTH are the near-term levers.
themes.driver: STLTECH's $1.1bn hyperscaler ramp against germanium/helium supply constraints and the raised 23% margin / 50% DC-mix guides; tariff-hike flow-through; 5G/FTTH capex; tower tenancy adds.
